bullets: How to prove triangles congruent with SSS and ASA, scale lengths, areas and volumes in similar figures, and use the circle theorems for semicircles, centre angles and the alternate segment
slides.heading: E-Math geometry: congruence, similarity and circle theorems
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we prove triangles congruent, scale similar figures, work through three circle theorems, and finish by untangling area from congruence.

bullets: Prove two triangles congruent using SSS and ASA and scale lengths, areas and volumes for similar figures
Use the angle in a semicircle, the centre-angle theorem and the alternate segment theorem
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A long thin rectangle and a square can both have area 36 cm² - are they the same shape?
What would you need to check before calling two shapes identical?
slides.heading: Same area - same shape?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the scenes will give us exact tests for sameness instead of guessing from area.

bullets: Congruent means every matching side and angle equal; SSS and ASA are two short tests that guarantee it
Similar figures share angles; if lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³
slides.heading: Congruence tests, similarity ratios and circle theorems
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: congruence is exact sameness, similarity is same shape at a different size, and the circle theorems turn arcs into angles.

bullets: Match the three sides of one triangle against the three sides of the other, pair by pair
When all three pairs are equal, the triangles are forced into exactly the same shape
slides.heading: SSS: three sides match
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: watch each side of the first triangle light up against its matching side, until all three pairs agree and the triangles sit exactly on top of each other.

bullets: Match two angles and the side between them in each triangle
The two angles fix the direction of the other sides, so the triangles must be congruent
slides.heading: ASA: two angles and the side between
slides.notes: Follow the scene: the two marked angles open the same way in both triangles, and the side trapped between them has the same length, leaving no room for a different third vertex.

bullets: Double every length and the shape stays the same while the area grows four times
Scale factor k for lengths gives k² for areas and k³ for volumes
slides.heading: Similarity: lengths, areas and volumes
slides.notes: Watch the smaller figure grow: each side doubles, the tiles covering it multiply by four, and the cubes filling it multiply by eight - same shape, new size.

bullets: Any angle standing on the diameter, with its vertex on the circle, is 90°
Spot the diameter first, then the angle on the circumference is a right angle
slides.heading: Angle in a semicircle is a right angle
slides.notes: Narrate the scene: the point slides around the semicircle and the angle at the circumference stays locked at a right angle wherever it stops.

bullets: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same chord
Halve the centre angle to get the circumference angle on the same arc
slides.heading: Centre angle = 2 × circumference angle
slides.notes: Follow the two angles as the scene builds them on the same chord: every time the circumference angle grows, the centre angle grows by exactly double.

bullets: The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment
Find the tangent, follow the chord, then read the angle in the segment on the far side
slides.heading: The alternate segment theorem
slides.notes: Watch the tangent touch the circle and the chord leave the point of contact: the angle outside the circle matches the angle inside the far segment.

bullets: A 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle and a 6 cm by 6 cm square both have area 36 cm²
Their sides and angles do not match, so equal area alone never proves congruence
slides.heading: A common mistake: same area means congruent?
slides.notes: Compare the two shapes side by side in the scene: the areas agree, but overlaying them shows sides sticking out - sameness needs matching sides and angles, not just area.

bullets: Triangles with sides 5, 7, 9 and 7, 9, 5: pair the equal sides in order
All three pairs match, so the triangles are congruent by SSS
slides.heading: Worked example: proving congruence with SSS
slides.notes: Work through the pairing on the board: write each side of one triangle beside its equal partner in the other, then state the SSS conclusion.

bullets: Try the worksheet questions in pairs: one congruence proof, one similarity scaling, two circle angles
Be ready to name the test or theorem you used for each answer
slides.heading: Your turn: prove, scale and use the theorems
slides.notes: Circulate while they work and listen for anyone arguing from area alone; ask them which sides and angles they have actually matched.

bullets: Four short questions on congruence tests, similarity ratios and circle theorems
Work on your own - this checks what stuck from the lesson
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Hand out the exit ticket and give them the last minutes in silence; collect them in to see who still equates area with congruence.
